clue.text: Take a town's advice and never be short of a drink

definitions.text: Take a town's advice and never be short of a drink

parts.words: Take a town's advice and never be short of a drink
parts.note: the Cheshire town's name, split in two, reads as an instruction to keep a supply of the fortified wine from Portugal

explanation.surface: Advice from a town council: always keep a bottle in.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the town's name into STOCK and PORT and it becomes advice: stock port, so you never run short of that drink. STOCKPORT is a town near Manchester.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue reads the Greater Manchester town's name as a command to keep the fortified wine in store.

clue.text: One inexperienced in Conservative reform

indicators.note: to reform is to reshape, so the letters of the party word are rebuilt in a new order

parts.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A novice politician takes part in reforming the Conservatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conservative' is not used as it stands: it gives TORY, Britain's everyday name for a Conservative, and 'reform' rearranges those four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyro is a beginner or novice, someone new to a skill.

clue.text: Gets wind of it going round on a bike

definitions.text: Gets wind of it going round on a bike

parts.words: Gets wind of it going round on a bike
parts.note: a rotating storm is wind going round, and the word begins with the letters of a bicycle, a cycle, followed by one

explanation.surface: Someone hears a rumour about a person riding around on a bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets wind of' looks like 'hears about', but the clue means real wind that spins round; the start of the word looks like cycle, as in riding a bike.
explanation.definitionFit: A cyclone is a storm whose winds spiral around a low-pressure centre.

clue.text: Gives support in setting the scene

definitions.meaning: holds up or bolsters something that might fall
in a theatre the stage props are put up to dress the set

explanation.surface: A stagehand helps out while the set is being arranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Propping something up means supporting it; putting stage properties in place sets a theatre scene.

clue.text: Artifice sure to be found out

indicators.note: read as worked out differently, these words tell us the letters of sure are rearranged

explanation.surface: A trick that is bound to be discovered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found out' sounds like being exposed, but here it tells you to rearrange SURE.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruse is a trick or stratagem, the same thing as an artifice.

clue.text: Doesn't make the grade as a flag bearer

definitions.meaning: falls short of the required level
the person carrying a flag stands beneath the standard, the banner

explanation.surface: A soldier fails his test while carrying the colours.
explanation.walkthrough: A standard is a flag, so the one holding it is literally under the standard.
explanation.definitionFit: Work below the required level is substandard; a bearer holds the banner, or standard, above their head.

clue.text: Tied by a moral obligation?

parts.note: being tied suggests bonds or ropes, but the binding here is a duty of conscience

explanation.surface: Someone feels tied down by a sense of duty.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the play on 'tied': no rope is involved, only a sense of duty.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes being obliged by one's integrity or a promise, as if bound by it.

clue.text: Animal barring the way

parts.note: a striped African beast lies across a road, which is also the black-and-white striped walkway pedestrians use

explanation.surface: A creature blocks the road.
explanation.walkthrough: A ZEBRA CROSSING is the British pedestrian crossing painted with black and white stripes across the road, like a zebra's coat.
explanation.definitionFit: The striped British road crossing takes its name from the black-and-white beast and runs across the carriageway.

clue.text: Going, going, but never gone

parts.note: the auctioneer's call is cut short so that it continues without end

explanation.surface: An auction where the final hammer never falls.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue borrows an auctioneer's 'Going, going, gone!' and drops the end, so the going never stops.
explanation.definitionFit: Something perpetual keeps on going forever and never comes to an end.

clue.text: One hoping not to miss the post

definitions.text: One hoping not to miss the post

parts.words: One hoping not to miss the post
parts.note: it reads as someone racing the mail collection, but the post is a job vacancy

explanation.surface: Someone hurries to catch the last collection of mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the post' looks like the mail; it is a job, and the person hoping for it has applied.
explanation.definitionFit: A candidate for a job puts in an application and hopes to be appointed.

clue.text: Sufficient lor a poet, no two ways about it

indicators.note: the two compass points go around the other word, so about signals one piece placed inside

parts.note: ways can be compass directions, here E (east) and W (west)
taken as written

explanation.surface: An undeniably adequate verse writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no two ways about it' sounds like 'certainly'; it means E and W, two compass directions, placed around NO.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic word for enough survives mainly in poetry, so it is plenty in a versifier's vocabulary.

clue.text: Creature sounding sweet, not to say dear

indicators.note: the word for the dessert, pronounced, gives the letters entered, so sounding marks a soundalike

parts.note: a mousse is a light whipped dessert, a sweet

explanation.surface: An animal said to be sweet, or even dear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not to say dear' is a second pun: the animal is a deer, which sounds like 'dear'.
explanation.definitionFit: The moose is a large North American deer, an animal.

clue.text: Such flattery won't wash? But it does

definitions.text: Such flattery won't wash? But it does

parts.words: Such flattery won't wash? But it does
parts.note: smooth flattery is called soft sawder, and the word for it is also the bar that cleans

explanation.surface: A protest that buttering someone up will not work.
explanation.walkthrough: Flattery is 'soft soap'; 'won't wash' means won't be believed, yet the cleaning bar does wash.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft soap is smooth flattery, and the cleansing bar used with water does literally wash.

clue.text: Quick on the bite?

definitions.meaning: inclined to give small bites, as a dog that nips

explanation.surface: A fish that is fast to take the bait.
explanation.definitionFit: Nippy means fast-moving, and also describes something apt to give little bites.

clue.text: Solitary one over fifty-one

parts.note: a means one, as in a single thing
L is the Roman numeral for fifty, followed by ONE as written

explanation.surface: A lone figure sits above a group of fifty-one.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts A above the rest; L is fifty in Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: Being by oneself, with no company, is to be solitary.

clue.text: Inactive in a situation I've acquired

indicators.note: the situation word gains the letters that follow, so acquired joins the next piece onto it

parts.note: a pass is a state of affairs, as in 'things have come to a pretty pass'
taken as written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone finds themselves stuck doing nothing in a situation they got into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a situation' is a 'pass', as in 'a pretty pass', a bad state of affairs.
explanation.definitionFit: Passive means not acting, simply letting things happen.

clue.text: Handy lubricant?

parts.note: grease slipped into someone's hand smooths the way, as a bribe does

explanation.surface: A slippery product kept within reach.
explanation.walkthrough: Palm oil is a real vegetable oil, and also slang for a bribe, money pressed into the palm to make things go smoothly.
explanation.definitionFit: The tropical vegetable fat is literally a greasy substance, and figuratively a bribe placed in the hand.

clue.text: A priest finds it hard going on foot

indicators.note: the letters of the churchman struggle into a new order, so this phrase signals an anagram

explanation.surface: A clergyman struggles when he has to walk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finds it hard' rearranges A PRIEST; the phrase sits next to 'going', tempting you to read 'hard going' as one idea.
explanation.definitionFit: To traipse is to walk wearily or trudge about.

clue.text: Mournful note on Gaelic translation

indicators.note: the rearranged word follows after the musical letter, so on joins them in order

parts.note: E is one of the musical notes A to G

indicators.note: translating changes the language, so the letters of Gaelic are reworked

explanation.surface: A sad tune is played over a Gaelic translation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'translation' rearranges the letters of Gaelic and 'on' sets them after the musical note; 'note' is one of the letters A to G.
explanation.definitionFit: Elegiac describes the tone of a lament for the dead: sorrowful.

clue.text: What's informative to one boy is applicable to the whole class

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
Eric is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A lesson aimed at one pupil turns out to suit everybody.
explanation.walkthrough: GEN is British slang for information, as in 'get the gen'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something generic relates to a whole group or kind rather than to a single member.

clue.text: City of low gags in variety

indicators.note: variety means a different arrangement, so the letters of the comic phrase are mixed up

explanation.surface: A city known for cheap jokes in music-hall shows.
explanation.walkthrough: Variety also means music-hall entertainment, so 'low gags in variety' reads as a comedian's act.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasgow is Scotland's largest city.

clue.text: District a short way south of 23

parts.note: Rd is the short form of road, a way

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood a little way south of another place.
explanation.walkthrough: '23' is the answer to 23-across, County Down in Northern Ireland, where the Ards district lies.
explanation.definitionFit: Ards is a local government area of County Down in Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Refreshments about ten, it's stated

indicators.note: the drinks word goes around the Roman numeral, so about signals one piece inside another

parts.note: teas are light refreshments
X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: Snacks are served at around ten o'clock, so it is said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's stated' looks like 'so it is said', but it defines: Texas is a US state.
explanation.definitionFit: Texas is one of the states of the USA, so it has been made a state.

clue.text: Swallow a county

definitions.meaning: to gulp a drink in one go
one of the six counties of Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: A bird flies over a county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swallow' looks like the bird; it is the verb, to drink quickly. Down is a county of Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: To gulp a drink in one is to sink it; County Down lies in Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Devotion to Zambia's capital brew of beer

indicators.note: a capital is the first, upper-case letter, so this takes the initial of the country
brewing mixes things up, so the letters of the beer are stirred into a new order

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: A fondness for Zambia's capital's local beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' looks like a city (Lusaka), but it is Zambia's first letter, Z; 'brew of' rearranges ALE, a beer, to EAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeal is passionate dedication or enthusiasm for a cause.

clue.text: She is on the look-out

indicators.note: is sits on, that is after, the look word, so on puts the two pieces in order

parts.note: lo is an old call meaning look, used to point something out

explanation.surface: A woman keeps watch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'look-out' looks like a sentry, but its first part is the old exclamation 'lo!' meaning look; 'on' places 'is' after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lois is a woman's name, so it can stand for 'she'.

clue.text: Liberate energy-a matter of debate when very cold

parts.note: to liberate is to set free
zing is liveliness or vigour
a point is an item argued in a discussion

explanation.surface: Freeing up energy is argued over during a cold spell.
explanation.definitionFit: The temperature at which water turns to ice is the moment it becomes icy cold.

clue.text: As horology students become with the passing of time

definitions.text: As horology students become with the passing of time

parts.words: As horology students become with the passing of time
parts.note: students of timepieces grow wise about them, and hands move round in a fixed direction as time passes

explanation.surface: Watchmaking pupils grow knowledgeable as the years go by.
explanation.walkthrough: Horology is the study of clocks; students become 'clock-wise', knowing about clocks, and hands turn this way as time passes.
explanation.definitionFit: Clock hands sweep round in this direction, and a student of timepieces becomes knowledgeable about them.
